definition: In computer vision and 3D computer graphics, the pinhole camera model describes the mathematical relationship between the coordinates of a point in three-dimensional space and its projection onto the image plane of an ideal pinhole camera, where the camera aperture is described as a point and no lenses are used to focus light.
details: The model does not include, for example, geometric distortions or blurring of unfocused objects caused by lenses and finite area apertures. It also does not take into account that most practical cameras have only discrete image coordinates (pixel indices). This means that the pinhole camera model can only be used as a first order approximation of the mapping from a 3D scene to an image plane. Its validity depends on the quality of the camera and, in general, decreases from the center to the edges of the image, as lens distortion effects increase. Some of the effects that the pinhole camera model does not take into account can be compensated, for example by applying suitable coordinate transformations on the image coordinates; other effects are sufficiently small to be neglected if a high quality camera is used. This means that the pinhole camera model often can be used as a reasonable description of how a camera depicts a 3D scene.

explainer.lead: It is the standard math for mapping a 3D point to where it lands on an image, and it underpins most camera geometry in vision and graphics. Its simplicity makes it useful even though real cameras depart from it.

tiers.eli5: Imagine light passing through a tiny hole in a box and landing on the back wall — the pinhole model says where each spot of light appears.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to build projection matrices and estimate camera pose or 3D structure, then add lens-distortion terms. A common pitfall is trusting it near image edges, where lens effects make it less accurate.
tiers.paperLevel: A 3D point projects to image coordinates proportional to its X and Y divided by its depth Z, scaled by focal length; it ignores lens distortion, defocus blur, and discrete pixel indices, so it is only a first-order approximation.

explainer.example: A point at depth 10 metres and 1 metre off-axis maps to an image offset of focal length divided by 10, giving a small displacement from the image centre.
